Native speakers' perception is that these pairs differ in stress only ... Stress is mostly found in penultimate syllables, although it can also be found in the antepenultimate and in the last syllable of a word (as in some of the examples above). [p. 77:] Regarding stress, it has been analyzed as phonemic, as in most descriptions of Guahiban languages. The rules of stress assignment have not been defined yet ... However, it is most often found in the penultimate syllable, although stress in the last and in the antepenultimate syllables is also possible.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is treated as phonemic (lexically contrastive, with segmentally identical minimal pairs), with a strong default/tendency for the penultimate syllable; antepenultimate and final stress also occur. The author suspects Sikuani-like weight tendencies (a heavy antepenult attracts stress, otherwise penult) and morphological conditioning (unstressed suffixes shift stress rightward within the root, stressed suffixes take primary stress: ['i.bo] 'stone' > [i.'bo.ta] > [i.bo.mi.'hi.ta]), but states that assignment rules cannot yet be established. Correlates: high pitch (typical penult case) and vowel lengthening (esp. non-penult stress), occasionally intensity; no vowel reduction, syllable-timed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; only 'primary stress' is mentioned in connection with stressed suffixes taking primary stress from the root (p. 70); no secondary-stress pattern given.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult-stressed trisyllables may be root+classifier/suffix (['jam.xɯ.ta] 'gun', ['huɾ.pa.bo] 'fish hook'); final-stressed words may be prefix+monosyllabic root ([pe.'hã] 'blood', [pe.'wi] 'meat') or carry a stressed suffix ([pu.pu.'ɾa] 'soup', [pe.tap̚.ta.'pa] 'pants'); vowel deletion can move stress (sec. 4); analysis explicitly 'preliminary'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in elicited citation forms (wordlist elicitation, Praat figures of isolated words daütjü, nekona, peha, nühü); phrase-level prosody not treated. Author notes phonetic correlate itself is unsettled (pitch vs length vs intensity).
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Yamalero (Yamarero/Mayaraxi), the Guahiban variety spoken by c. 300 people incl. ethnic Yaruro in the Caño Mochuelo reserve (Casanare, Colombia), not Playero of the Río Arauca proper. Glottolog 5.x files Ginebra 2022 under play1240 Playero; Ginebra (pp. 23-24) follows Queixalós 1993 and Fabre 1998 in treating Yamarero and Playero as one variety / a former single group and finds Playero the lexically closest variety, while noting Yamalero also shares Cuiba-like traits (codas). Earlier authors (Kerr & Berg 1973, Kondo 1982) grouped Mayaraxi with Cuiba (cuib1242). No separate glottocode exists for Yamalero.
